tier_reason: README Performance section gives first-party FN-DSA cycle tables (i5-8259U, Cortex-A76, SiFive U74; Rust 1.97.1) from public benches (fn-dsa/benches/*.rs), but the OpenSSL RSA-2048 comparison is prose-only ratios with no RSA cycle counts, no OpenSSL version/flags and no benchmark harness for the baseline, so it cannot reach A; not peer-reviewed, so not B.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Prose only, no RSA numbers on page: on i5-8259U (x86_64) FN-DSA/512 is 'about as fast as RSA-2048 for verification, but about 2.5x faster for signature generation, and many times faster for key pair generation'; on the ARM Cortex-A76 'signature generation with this code is about 8 times faster than OpenSSL's RSA-2048'; FN-DSA/512 is said to be 'substantially faster than RSA-2048 on all these systems' except x86_64 verify parity. FN-DSA/512 cycles on i5-8259U: keygen 8.91M, sign 1.13M, verify 63.3K.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Rust 1.97.1 (rustc) for the i5-8259U table (toolchain for ARM/RISC-V tables not stated); cargo bench harness in fn-dsa/benches (keygen.rs, sign.rs, verify.rs) reading rdtsc / pmccntr_el0 / rdcycle; AVX2 path auto-selected at runtime on x86_64, NEON on aarch64; RUSTFLAGS/target-cpu not stated; OpenSSL build/version/flags for the RSA-2048 comparison not stated
corrections.caveats: The OpenSSL RSA-2048 comparison is a prose claim ('about 8 times faster', 'about 2.5x') with no RSA cycle table, OpenSSL version or flags, and the repo's benches do not run OpenSSL, so it is a first-party claim with partial methodology, not a reproducible A/B benchmark. Per the README, no FN-DSA draft has been published yet and the 2026-07-22 update implements a 'best guess' at the upcoming draft; keys/signatures are expected to break compatibility before v1.0. Unlicense (public-domain dedication): no patent grant.

notes: Metadata verified via gh: Unlicense, not archived/fork, 66 stars, last commit 2026-07-30 (active). Numbers and the 8x / 2.5x / parity phrasing match the README exactly; only the caveats/flags were sharpened.

tier_reason: Upgraded C->B: the paper was peer-reviewed and published at ESORICS 2024 (LNCS, DOI 10.1007/978-3-031-70890-9_7, pp. 123-143), and its Table 2 shows 1.30-1.64x cycle-count wins over the pq-crystals Kyber AVX2 code (GCC 9.4.0, Xeon Platinum 8475B). It falls short of A because no code has been released (searched GitHub) and compiler flags are not stated.

corrections.baseline: pq-crystals Kyber 'standard' branch AVX2 implementation (FIPS 203 draft code, the paper's ref [5]) for ML-KEM cycle counts; liboqs 0.10.1 ML-KEM AVX2 via OQS-provider on OpenSSL 3.3.0-dev for TLS 1.3 handshakes/sec
corrections.claimed_speedup: AVX-512 ML-KEM is 1.30x-1.64x faster than the AVX2 implementation in median CPU cycles (max 1.64x for ML-KEM-1024 Encaps: 25,062 vs 41,162 cycles). Batched keygen (8 keys) gives 4.9x / 4.2x / 3.5x for ML-KEM-512/768/1024 per the paper. TLS 1.3 handshake gains are small, about 0.4-5.6% more connections/sec in most PQ-only and hybrid configurations (derived from page data), and the paper itself calls them 'subtle' / 'minimal'.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: GCC 9.4.0 (optimization flags not stated); AVX-512 disabled when benchmarking the AVX2 baseline; Turbo Boost and hyper-threading left on; median of 100,000 runs; TLS tests with OpenSSL 3.3.0-dev + OQS provider (openssl s_server / s_time)
corrections.caveats: Published at ESORICS 2024 (LNCS), but the paper only says 'we will later open source our code' and no public repository was found (GitHub repo and code search), so has_code=false and the result cannot be reproduced. Table 3 has one cell where AVX-512 is slower (ML-KEM-1024/Dilithium5: 2451.08 vs 3191.46 conn/s, an AVX2 value that duplicates the Falcon512 cell, so possibly a copy error). The stated batch-keygen ratios are a little higher than the table implies against non-batched AVX-512 keygen (about 4.7x / 4.0x / 3.4x, derived from page data). Handshake gains are within about 6%.

notes: Hardware and compiler claims check out; the baseline for the headline 1.64x is the pq-crystals standard-branch AVX2 code, not liboqs itself (liboqs 0.10.1 is only the integration target), so I corrected baseline to say so and left baseline_in_list=true because the TLS comparison runs through liboqs. The tier is upgraded to B on the confirmed ESORICS 2024 publication.

tier_reason: docs/performance.md gives first-party best-of-three timings for the C backend next to `openssl speed` (OpenSSL 3.6.4) on named CPUs (Apple M1 Pro, Ryzen AI 9 HX PRO 370). The bench code (bench/bench_curve448.ml) is public, but the C compiler and version are not stated, flags are only dune's :standard, and OpenSSL is timed by a different harness, so this is C, not A.

corrections.workload: Single-operation X448 key exchange, Ed448 key pair from seed, and Ed448 sign/verify of a 64-byte message (Ed448ph is not benchmarked). Best of three 1-second runs of the project's OCaml bench (bench/bench_curve448.ml, via the OCaml bindings), compared against `openssl speed` numbers for OpenSSL 3.6.4 on the same machine. Keypair-from-seed has no OpenSSL figure.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: C backend stubs built with dune --profile release using OCaml's :standard C flags (lib/c/dune), with GCC or Clang (compiler and version not stated); OCaml 5.4.1 (M1 Pro) / 5.5.1 (Ryzen); baseline OpenSSL 3.6.4 via `openssl speed` (its build flags not stated)
corrections.stars_or_usage: 0 stars (repo created 2026-09-13; not yet published to opam)
corrections.caveats: Results are mixed, not a clean win: X448 is only about 2% faster on the M1 Pro (130 vs 133 us); Ed448 sign is about 7% slower than OpenSSL on the M1 Pro; Ed448 verify is always slower (1.26-1.44x, derived from page data) because the C backend is constant-time and OpenSSL uses variable-time double-scalar multiplication. The project timings go through the OCaml FFI with its own gettimeofday loop while OpenSSL uses `openssl speed`, so the harnesses differ. The project is brand new (0 stars, not on opam) with no independent review, and the C compiler/version are not stated. LICENSE.md is ISC for project code; the vendored C pieces are MIT/ISC (fiat-crypto, BoringSSL, tiny_sha3).

notes: gh shows license NOASSERTION only because LICENSE.md adds a third-party table; the project code is ISC and the vendored C is MIT/ISC, so copyable is correct. Last commit is 2026-09-26 (active), 0 stars, not a fork. All page numbers match the record.
